title: OpenAI's Jalapeño inference chip publishes first benchmarks — 1.5–1.9x Blackwell per watt
subtitle: At Hot Chips 2026, OpenAI and Broadcom disclosed independently verified numbers against three public models and confirmed a small-volume 2026 rollout scaling in 2027.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: At the Hot Chips 2026 conference in Palo Alto, OpenAI presented the first published performance results for Jalapeño, its Broadcom-co-designed custom inference chip. On SemiAnalysis's public InferenceX benchmark, run against three public AI models, Jalapeño delivered 1.5 to 1.9 times more work per watt than an Nvidia Blackwell system while cutting end-to-end latency by 1.7 to 3.6 times. OpenAI said deployment begins in very small volumes by the end of 2026 with material scale-up in 2027. The chip has not yet been benchmarked against Nvidia's forthcoming Vera Rubin generation.

The reason this matters is not that Nvidia has been dethroned — it hasn't — but that a hyperscaler now has publishable, third-party-verified numbers showing a custom part beating a Blackwell rack on inference economics. That is the argument OpenAI has been making privately to its board and its infrastructure partners for over a year: that inference is a different workload from training, and that owning the silicon for it changes unit economics enough to justify the R&D bill. The Hot Chips paper turns that argument into a public artifact.

The disclosure lands the same day Nvidia reported $96.2 billion in quarterly revenue and told the market it has supply for another 70% growth year. Both things can be true at once. Training demand keeps compounding, and Nvidia keeps capturing it; inference is where the margin fight lives, and where every large model provider — OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Alibaba — is racing to route around Nvidia. Jalapeño is OpenAI's opening move in that fight, and it worked: the number is public, and it wins on the metric it was designed for.

For learners: benchmarks are marketing until they are reproducible. What made this announcement land was that SemiAnalysis's InferenceX suite is public, the three models tested are public, and the methodology can be re-run by anyone with a Blackwell system. When you evaluate a chip claim — or any AI capability claim — check whether the eval, the model, and the harness are all things you could run yourself. If any of the three is proprietary, treat the number accordingly.
